title: I Am: context and text
short: Written in the Northampton asylum, probably late 1844 or 1845, and first printed in 1848; this text is from Blunden and Porter's 1920 edition.
body: Clare was confined from 1837 in Dr Matthew Allen's asylum at High Beach in Epping Forest, walked home from it in July 1841, and in December 1841 was committed to the Northampton General Lunatic Asylum, where he lived until his death in 1864. The poem survives in a transcript by W. F. Knight, the asylum's house steward from 1845 to 1850, who copied many of Clare's later poems. It is usually said to have first appeared in the Bedford Times on 1 January 1848, and Frederick Martin's Life (1865) printed it with variants. The standard text is in Robinson and Powell's Later Poems (1984); Blunden and Porter's 1920 selection, the source here, brought much of Clare's manuscript verse to twentieth-century readers.

title: 'I AM'
short: The capitalised assertion of being echoes God's name in Exodus 3:14, 'I AM THAT I AM', and perhaps the philosopher's 'I think, therefore I am'.
body: At the burning bush God tells Moses, 'I AM THAT I AM ... say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you' (Exodus 3:14). Clare's capitals give the bare fact of his existence an almost sacred weight, and the next words, 'yet what I am none cares or knows', shrink it to a lonely fact without recognition. The poem asserts existence, not identity, and it ends by imagining the self returned to its 'Creator'. Readers have also compared Descartes' cogito, though the poem argues nothing philosophically. Bate took the phrase as the title of his 2003 selection.

anchor: My friends forsake me like a memory lost
title: 'My friends forsake me'
short: The friends' desertion echoes Job and the Psalms, where the sufferer is forgotten by kin and friends.
body: Job complains, 'My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me' (Job 19:14), and the Psalmist, 'I am forgotten as a dead man out of mind' (Psalm 31:12). Clare had been celebrated in 1820 as the Northamptonshire peasant poet and was now largely forgotten, with few visitors. The simile turns round: it is not that he forgets them, but that they let him go, as one loses a memory.

sources.cite: The Holy Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, 1611

title: 'self-consumer'
greek: Latin consumere, to use up, devour
short: He alone must consume, eat up or use up, his sorrows, with no one to share them; there may be a glance at wasting illness.
body: The compound means that his woes have no outlet but himself: he digests his own grief. 'Consume' (Latin consumere, to use up, devour) also carried the sense of wasting away, as in 'consumption', so the phrase hints that grief eats him as he eats it. The coinage has the compressed force of Clare's late style. It also reverses the usual relation of poet and reader: the poet who once had a public now has no audience for his sorrows but himself.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. the headword

title: 'oblivious host'
greek: Latin oblivio, forgetfulness; hostis, enemy, army
short: His woes come and go like a forgotten crowd; 'oblivious' may carry the older sense of 'causing forgetfulness', like Lethe.
body: A 'host' is a multitude, originally an army (from Latin hostis). 'Oblivious' could mean forgetful or, in an older sense, bringing forgetfulness. The woes 'rise and vanish' without being remembered, a crowd that leaves no trace. The word prepares for 'death's oblivion' in the next line and suggests the shades who drink from Lethe in Virgil's underworld. Like the 'memory lost' of l. 2, the woes vanish into forgetting, so that even suffering fails to give the self a lasting shape.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. the headword
Virgil, Aeneid 6 (the shades at the Styx, ll. 295-330, and at Lethe, ll. 703-51)

anchor: Like shades in love and death's oblivion lost
title: 'Like shades'
short: His sorrows are like ghosts lost in forgetfulness, as in the classical underworld; 'love' suggests lost loves among them.
body: 'Shades' are the spirits of the dead in classical epic, and Clare's woes, like the crowding shades by the Styx in Aeneid 6, are restless and unremembered. The line pairs love and death as twin forms of oblivion, perhaps thinking of Mary Joyce, his early love, who had died in 1838 without his knowing it. The repetition of 'lost' at the ends of ll. 2 and 5 is an identical rhyme that presses on the idea of loss.

title: 'shadows tost'
short: He lives tossed among shadows, like the shades or like a ship in a storm, preparing the sea and shipwreck of stanza 2.
body: 'Tost' is the older spelling of 'tossed' and suggests being thrown about by waves. 'And yet I am' reasserts existence against everything in the stanza. The sentence then runs on across the stanza break ('tost / Into the nothingness'), an unusual enjambment that enacts the tossing it describes. The word belongs to the idiom of hymns and of the Psalms, where the soul is tossed on troubled waters, and Clare's late verse often stays close to hymn language.

anchor: the nothingness of scorn and noise
title: 'scorn and noise'
short: Probably the world of the asylum: contempt and constant clamour that empty life of meaning.
body: A public asylum with many patients was a noisy place, and Clare often wrote of being mocked or ignored. 'Nothingness' is a strong abstract word, a void filled only with scorn and noise. Bate's biography describes his life at Northampton, including the relative freedom of his early years there, when he could walk into the town, and his deep sense of being cut off.

sources.cite: Jonathan Bate, John Clare: A Biography (London, 2003), chapters on High Beach and the Northampton asylum
The Victorian Web: John Clare, biography

anchor: the living sea of waking dreams
title: 'living sea of waking dreams'
short: Life feels like a sea of hallucination or daydream, where waking and dreaming are confused.
body: 'Waking dreams' suggests both the delusions recorded in Clare's asylum years (he sometimes claimed to be Byron, and believed he had two wives) and a general sense of living in unreality. The 'sea' prepares for the 'shipwreck' of l. 10. 'Living' is paradoxical: this sea is alive, yet it holds 'neither sense of life nor joys'. The two halves of the phrase pull against each other: 'living' and 'waking' promise reality, while 'sea' and 'dreams' dissolve it.

anchor: the vast shipwreck of my life's esteems
title: 'shipwreck of my life's esteems'
short: 'Esteems' are what he valued and the esteem others had for him; all have been wrecked like a ship at sea.
body: The plural 'esteems' is unusual. It can mean the things he held dear, his values and hopes, and also the regard of others, his reputation. His fame of the 1820s, his family life and his home village were all lost. Shipwreck is a common figure in poems of despair, and a comparable case is Cowper's 'The Castaway', written in Cowper's last depression, though no direct borrowing is proven. Clare admired Cowper and echoes him elsewhere, as Vincent Newey has shown.

title: 'een the dearest'
short: 'Een' is 'e'en', even. 'The dearest' may be his wife Patty and their children, or Mary Joyce, his first love; readers differ.
body: Clare married Martha ('Patty') Turner in 1820 and they had seven children; she is not known to have visited him at Northampton. Yet in his asylum delusions he thought of Mary Joyce, his childhood love, as his first wife, and wrote poems and letters to her. Bate stresses how both women haunt the late poems. The poem need not settle the question: the dearest have become 'strange', 'nay, rather stranger than the rest', because illness and confinement have estranged him from everyone.

anchor: scenes where man has never trod
title: 'where man has never trod'
short: He longs for untouched nature without human presence, a Romantic ideal of solitude (compare Byron's 'pathless woods').
body: After the stanza of loss, the last stanza turns to longing for a place without men or women, alone with God. It recalls Romantic longing for wild solitude, such as Byron's 'There is a pleasure in the pathless woods' (Childe Harold IV, st. 178). Clare identified strongly with Byron, and in 1841 wrote his own 'Child Harold' and 'Don Juan'. The untrodden place can also be read as Eden before the Fall, or as the grave.

sources.cite: Lord Byron, Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto IV (1818), st. 178

anchor: A place where woman never smiled or wept
title: 'woman never smiled or wept'
short: The wish to escape women's smiles and tears may reflect his losses in love; he wants a world without emotional ties.
body: Paired with 'man' in l. 13, 'woman' completes the rejection of human company. The line suggests the pain that love and family had brought him, with Mary Joyce and Patty in the background. It may also recall Eden before Eve, where Adam was alone with his maker (Genesis 2:18-22). 'Smiled or wept' covers the whole range of feeling, joy and sorrow alike, from which he now wishes to be free; the place he imagines is one without the claims of human affection.

title: 'my Creator, GOD'
short: The capitalised 'GOD' answers the capitalised 'I AM' of l. 1: the self no one knows hopes to be known by its maker.
body: The capitals pair the poem's opening and close, so that the 'I AM' whom nobody knows longs to 'abide' with the original I AM. 'Abide' has a biblical ring ('Abide in me, and I in you', John 15:4). The religious hope is simple and childlike, and leads straight into the memory of childhood sleep. The comma before 'GOD' makes the name a solemn apposition, spoken with emphasis.

sources.cite: The Holy Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, 1611

anchor: sleep as I in childhood sweetly slept
title: 'as I in childhood sweetly slept'
short: Death is imagined as a return to the untroubled sleep of childhood at Helpston, before fame and madness.
body: Clare's childhood in the village of Helpston, Northamptonshire, fed much of his poetry, and the enclosure of its open fields was one of his great losses. The wish to sleep as he slept then is a wish for death, softened into rest. The alliteration of 'sleep', 'sweetly' and 'slept' gives the line a lulling sound. Childhood is the last place in the poem where the 'I' felt whole.

title: 'Untroubling and untroubled'
short: He will neither trouble others nor be troubled: the paired active and passive forms suggest his sense of having been a burden.
body: The figure is polyptoton, the same word in different grammatical forms. It implies that he knows he has troubled others and wishes to be free both of causing and of suffering harm. 'Where I lie' gently names the grave. The paired words are slow and evenly weighted, and the repeated prefix 'un-' strips them down, as the whole last stanza strips life to a minimum of grass and sky. It is the poem's quietest line, with the rhythm of a lullaby, matching the childhood sleep of the line before.

sources.cite: Eric Robinson and David Powell, eds., John Clare (The Oxford Authors, 1984), text and notes

anchor: The grass below--above the vaulted sky
title: 'the vaulted sky'
short: The last line lays him in the grave between grass below and sky above; 'vaulted' makes the sky a church roof.
body: 'Vaulted' means arched, like the stone vault of a church, so the sky becomes the roof of nature's cathedral. The line is balanced around its dash, 'below' and 'above' turning on each other almost as a chiasmus. The poem resolves into peace found in nature and with God, not in human society. Grass over the dead is a biblical commonplace ('All flesh is grass', Isaiah 40:6), and it suits a poet of fields and hedgerows.

title: Form
short: Three six-line stanzas of iambic pentameter, rhymed ababcc (the first ababbb), the stanza of Shakespeare's Venus and Adonis.
body: Each sestet has a quatrain of alternate rhyme followed by a couplet, the form Shakespeare used in Venus and Adonis. Stanza 1 is irregular: its last two lines rhyme with lines 2 and 4 ('lost', 'host', 'lost', 'tost'), so the sound of loss dominates. The steady pentameter and regular stanzas give the poem a composed, almost classical calm that contrasts with its subject.
